title: Grade 1 Subtraction: How to Teach It, Step by Step (+ Free Quiz)
meta_desc: Grade 1 subtraction made simple: take-away, counting back, difference and fact families within 20, plus a free 8-question quiz and printable worksheets.
excerpt: Subtraction trips up more six-year-olds than addition ever does, mostly because we teach it as one idea when it is really three. Here is the order that works, plus a quick quiz to check where your child stands.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 1 child the sum 7 − 2 and most will get 5 without much fuss. Give them 12 − 9 and watch what happens: fingers come out, counting starts from one, and about half will confidently tell you the answer is 21. That gap is the whole story of Grade 1 subtraction. The problem is rarely the child — it is that we teach subtraction as a single skill when it is really three different ideas wearing the same minus sign. Good Grade 1 subtraction worksheets separate those ideas out and build them in order, and that is exactly what this guide walks through.

You need almost nothing to start: a small pile of counters (buttons, tamarind seeds, one-rupee coins), a strip of paper marked 0 to 20, and ten unhurried minutes. In my experience teaching six-year-olds, the counters matter more than any app.

Start with take-away within 10

The first and most concrete meaning of subtraction is take-away: you have some, you remove some, you count what is left. Put out 8 counters, ask your child to take away 3, then count the rest. Say it in words every time — ‘eight take away three leaves five’ — because the words are what eventually replace the counters.

Stay inside 10 until this is effortless. A child who can do the take-away sums to 10 without hesitating has the foundation for everything that follows. Rushing past this stage is the single most common mistake I see.

Counting back on the number line

Once take-away is solid, introduce counting back. On the 0–20 strip, put a finger on 9 and hop backwards three times — 8, 7, 6 — landing on 6. This is faster than removing counters and it builds the mental picture children carry for years.

One caution worth its own line: counting back only stays reliable when the second number is small. Ask a child to count back 8 from 15 and they will lose track around the third hop. So teach counting back for sums like 11 − 2 or 14 − 3, and reach for a smarter method when the number being taken away is large.

Subtraction as finding the difference

Here is the idea most Grade 1 worksheets skip, and it is the one that unlocks the rest. Subtraction does not always mean take-away. Sometimes it means difference — how much bigger one number is than another, or how far apart they sit. ‘Aarav has 9 marbles, Meera has 4, how many more does Aarav have?’ is a subtraction, 9 − 4, but nothing is being taken away.

Teach this by lining up two rows of counters and matching them one to one; the leftover counters in the longer row are the difference. Children who only ever meet take-away get genuinely stuck on ‘how many more’ word problems later, so plant this seed early.

Fact families: subtraction is addition backwards

The strongest tool in the whole of Grade 1 arithmetic is the fact family. The numbers 4, 5 and 9 make four related facts: 4 + 5 = 9, 5 + 4 = 9, 9 − 4 = 5, and 9 − 5 = 4. A child who knows their addition bonds can read subtraction straight off them — they think ‘4 plus what makes 9?’ instead of laboriously counting back.

This is why I always teach addition bonds to ten first. If your child already knows that 6 and 4 make 10, then 10 − 6 needs no counting at all. Subtraction stops being a separate mountain to climb and becomes the same mountain seen from the other side.

Crossing ten: subtraction within 20

The sums that break down — 13 − 5, 15 − 8, 12 − 9 — all cross the ten-line, and counting back fails here. Teach the make-ten method instead. For 15 − 8: first go back to 10 (that uses 5), then take away the remaining 3, landing on 7. It leans directly on the number bonds, which is the whole point.

The errors to watch for

A few mistakes show up again and again, and knowing them lets you catch trouble before it sets in:

  • Reversing the digits — answering 12 − 9 as 3 by doing 9 − 12 in disguise, or reading the sum right to left. Model that subtraction, unlike addition, cares about order.
  • Counting the start number — for 9 − 3, counting ‘9, 8, 7’ and stopping at 7. The first hop should be to 8, not 9.
  • Forgetting the special rules — that any number minus itself is 0, and any number minus 0 is unchanged. Two facts, a whole column of easy marks.

A worksheet progression that works

Order matters more than volume. A sensible week of Grade 1 subtraction worksheets moves like this: two days of take-away within 10, one day of counting back, one day of ‘how many more’ difference problems, and the weekend on mixed sums within 20 where the child must choose the method. That choosing step — deciding whether to count back or make ten — is where real fluency shows, not in speed drills. Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday every time.

Test what your child knows, then practise

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering exactly these ideas — take-away, counting back, difference, fact families and crossing ten. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable Grade 1 subtraction worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key you can reprint as often as you like.

quiz.title: Grade 1 Subtraction Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions covering take-away, counting back, difference and fact families. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Take away 2 from 6 and 4 are left.

questions.q: Count back 3 from 10. Where do you land?
questions.explanation: Hop back three times: 9, 8, 7. You land on 7.

questions.q: There are 8 birds on a wire and 5 fly away. How many are left?
Which fact belongs to the same family as 4 + 5 = 9?
questions.explanation: The numbers 4, 5 and 9 give 9 − 5 = 4 as part of the family.
Make ten: 15 − 5 = 10, then take away 1 more to get 9.

questions.q: Riya has 12 sweets and eats 4. How many are left?
questions.explanation: 12 − 4 = 8. Go back to 10, then take away 2 more.
Any number take away itself leaves nothing, so the answer is 0.

faq.q: Should Grade 1 subtraction come before or after addition?
faq.a: After. A child who knows addition bonds — especially the pairs that make ten — can read subtraction straight off them using fact families, instead of counting back every time. Get addition within 20 fairly secure first.

faq.q: Why does my child reverse subtraction and answer 12 − 9 as 3 the wrong way?
faq.a: Because addition does not care about order, so many children assume subtraction does not either. Show them with counters that 9 − 12 is impossible at this level — you cannot take 12 away from 9 — so the bigger number must come first.

faq.q: When should I stop letting my child count on fingers?
faq.a: Not by banning them — by giving better tools. As counting back, fact families and the make-ten method take hold, children drop fingers on their own because the strategies are faster. Fingers at the start are completely fine.

faq.q: What is the hardest part of Grade 1 subtraction?
faq.a: Sums that cross ten, such as 13 − 5 or 15 − 8, where counting back gets unreliable. The make-ten method — go back to 10 first, then take away the rest — is the fix, and it depends on knowing number bonds to ten.
